paragraphs.heading: A field made in the core
paragraphs.text: Earth's magnetic field stretches from deep inside the planet out into space, where it meets the solar wind, a stream of charged particles coming off the Sun. It is produced by electric currents in the outer core, where a mix of molten iron and nickel churns as heat escapes from the core. Scientists call this process a geodynamo. To a first approximation, the field looks like that of a giant bar magnet set through the middle of the planet, tilted about 11° from the axis Earth spins on.

paragraphs.heading: Poles that are not what they seem
paragraphs.text: The north geomagnetic pole, on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, is in fact the south pole of Earth's field. That sounds backwards, but opposite poles attract, and the north end of a compass needle is pulled toward it. The magnetic poles usually sit near the geographic poles and drift over geological time, though slowly enough that an ordinary compass still works. Every so often, at irregular intervals that average several hundred thousand years, the field flips and the two magnetic poles abruptly trade places.

paragraphs.heading: Strength and direction
paragraphs.text: The strength of the field differs from place to place and changes over time. In 2019 it measured about 60,000 nT over Siberia but only about 30,000 nT over Brazil. By comparison, a strong fridge magnet reaches about 100 G, while Earth's field is just 0.30 to 0.60 G. At any spot the field also has a direction in three dimensions. The angle between magnetic north and true north is called the declination, and the tilt of the field away from the horizontal is called the inclination, or dip.

paragraphs.heading: Dip from pole to equator
paragraphs.text: In the northern hemisphere the field points down into the ground. At the North Magnetic Pole it points straight down, and it tilts steadily upward as you move toward the magnetic equator, where it lies flat. Keep going south and it keeps turning until, at the South Magnetic Pole, it points straight up. Dip was once measured with a device called a dip circle, but magnetometers now do the job more reliably.

paragraphs.heading: A shield for the air
paragraphs.text: The space that the field controls is called the magnetosphere, and it reaches tens of thousands of kilometres out, above the ionosphere. It turns aside most of the solar wind, whose charged particles, along with cosmic rays, would otherwise strip off the upper atmosphere, including the ozone layer that blocks harmful ultraviolet light. One way air can be lost is for gas to get trapped in bubbles of magnetic field that the solar wind tears away. Calculations for Mars suggest that when its magnetic field faded, the planet lost nearly all of its atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A record kept in rock
paragraphs.text: Igneous rocks record which way the field pointed, so its flips show up as stripes on the sea floor, centred on mid-ocean ridges where the floor is spreading apart. Between flips the poles stay steady enough for these rocks to track how continents have moved. The flip pattern also lets geologists date rocks and sediments, a method called magnetostratigraphy. Because the field magnetizes the crust as well, unusual magnetic readings can point to deposits of metal ores, and living things from some bacteria to pigeons use the field to find their way.
